## Library entrance closure: Monday to Thursday

The library will remain open on its usual schedule, but the east entrance, facing the bus shelter, will be closed to everyone from Monday through Thursday while the pavement outside it is replaced. Please use the west entrance, facing the playground.

If you are coming from the playground, use the west entrance as normal. If you are coming from the bus shelter, follow the signed path along the south side of the building to the west entrance. This route adds approximately 120 metres to the journey. It has no steps, but one section crosses uneven ground covered by a temporary firm mat. The mat is on the route to the west entrance; the east entrance is closed to wheelchair users as well as all other visitors. The bus shelter will remain available, but the direct path from it to the east entrance will be behind a temporary barrier.

During library opening hours, staff can meet visitors at the bus shelter and accompany them to the west entrance. If you would like this assistance, call the library desk before setting out. You can also request assistance on arrival by calling the number displayed at the shelter, but a staff member may not be available immediately. The library cannot provide transport around the building.

The returns slot beside the east entrance will also be inaccessible. Books due Monday through Thursday may be returned on Friday without a late charge, including books borrowed from another branch.

Heavy rain may delay the work. If the closure lasts longer, an updated notice will be posted at both entrances and at the bus shelter. The Friday return arrangement will remain in place unless that notice announces a further extension.

The amber indicator on the curing-line monitor has appeared just after washdown on three of the last five morning shifts. It means the humidity probe’s reading is outside the range accepted by the controller; it does not establish whether the room is too humid or the probe is giving an unreliable reading. The display often called the “backup” measures temperature only, so a normal reading there cannot resolve a humidity question.

On all three mornings, the indicator cleared within twelve minutes. Operators wiped moisture from the outside of the probe housing on two mornings; on the third, nobody touched it. These observations are consistent with moisture around the housing, but they do not establish that wiping cleared the warning. The housing is not the sensing element. Wiping is recorded here as an observation, not recommended as a remedy.

For now, record when the indicator appears, when it clears, and whether washdown has finished. Do not open the housing. If the indicator remains amber after fifteen minutes, call the shift lead before starting the next batch. The lead may request a handheld humidity check using the unit in the instrument cabinet. A handheld reading does not authorize a restart; that decision remains with the shift lead.

Maintenance has been asked to inspect the seal at the next planned stop, but this request does not establish that the seal has failed. Continue recording mornings when no warning appears, using the log’s “no warning” box beside the time fields. Recording both warnings and mornings without warnings is necessary to establish how often the pattern occurs.

The shortcut saves a search only if the user knows where focus landed. We tested a spoken location cue to help screen-reader users return to a table after opening a note. In the cue version, closing the note spoke the current row label. In the existing version, keyboard focus returned to the same cell without the added cue.

Twelve experienced screen-reader users completed four tasks with each version. Six used the cue version first; six used the existing version first. They worked with different tables in the two task sets, and for half of each order group, the tables were assigned to versions in reverse. This reduced the alignment between version and practice, but could not rule out learning that carried from the first set of tasks into the second.

The median of participants’ mean completion times was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. That is a three-second difference between two medians, not the median of participants’ within-person differences. Seven participants had a lower personal mean time with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two were unchanged at the recorded precision. We have not calculated a confidence interval or performed a significance test. Timing began when participants closed the note and ended when they activated the requested table entry; reading the note was outside the timed interval.

Did the cue help users feel oriented? Nine participants said in the closing interview that it did. Four of those nine also described times when the cue interrupted speech they were still listening to. The other three participants did not report an orientation benefit, but none asked to remove the feature. That does not tell us whether they wanted it enabled by default; we did not ask.

The findings make an orientation benefit plausible for some users in these tasks. They also point to a design question: how should the cue behave when someone is still listening to speech? A next version could make it interruptible, but we did not implement or test that behavior, so these timings say nothing about its effects.

The evidence has limits. Participants were experienced screen-reader users, and the study does not show how less experienced users would respond. The prototype’s tables fit on one screen, so the study does not establish performance on larger tables. The next study should examine those conditions and how users manage the cue alongside ongoing speech.

The spoken cue says which row is active when a user returns from a note. Does that help them find the requested table entry? In this study, twelve experienced screen-reader users completed four tasks with the cue and four with the existing version, which returns keyboard focus to the same cell without speaking. Half used the cue version first. We used different tables in each set of tasks and reversed the table assignment for half of each order group.

The median of participants’ mean completion times was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. These are two medians, not the median of participants’ within-person differences. Seven participants had a lower mean time with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two had equal means at the recorded precision. We timed from closing the note to activating the requested table entry; reading the note was not included. We have not calculated a confidence interval or performed a significance test, so these timings do not establish a reliable difference.

The interviews suggest that the cue may help some users feel oriented. Nine participants said it helped, though four of those nine also recalled times when it interrupted speech they were still listening to. The other three participants did not report an orientation benefit. None asked to remove the feature, but we did not ask whether it should be enabled by default.

Does the cue help users without interrupting what they are listening to? The study leaves that question open. The order and table assignments reduced the alignment between version and practice, but some participants may have carried a search strategy from the first set of tasks into the second. We also recruited only experienced screen-reader users, and the prototype’s tables fit on one screen. The results do not tell us how less experienced users would respond or how the cue would work on large tables.

The growing waiting list calls for action, but we should distinguish between opening places and deciding how much disruption that requires. There are twenty full beds and ten households waiting. Dividing every returning gardener’s bed in half may seem a fair starting point: nobody wants access to depend on having been lucky enough to join years ago. Yet we are allocating more than land. We are also allocating the chance to keep crops through their growing cycles. For that reason, I support dividing vacant beds first and allowing returning gardeners to keep their present beds for one more season.

Four full beds will become vacant at the end of this season. Dividing them would create eight half beds, allowing eight offers to households on the waiting list. Assuming every offer is accepted, two households would remain without a bed. That is a real cost, and we should not describe the proposal as clearing the list. It would nevertheless open places for most waiting households without requiring every returning gardener to disrupt established planting at once.

Protecting established planting deserves scrutiny, because it can also protect an established advantage. A perennial cannot give its gardener a permanent claim to shared land. Our membership agreement promises a bed for a season, with renewal decided annually. The justification for one more season in an existing bed is therefore a limited transition, not an entitlement to continued possession. The committee would publish the following season’s allocation rule before renewals open, so that this temporary arrangement does not become a permanent rule by default.

That published rule must cover new members as well as returning ones. A household accepting a half bed also needs notice of any future decision to merge, move, or resize it. Otherwise, we risk recreating the uncertainty we are trying to reduce. I do not yet have a preferred permanent bed size. We can decide how to manage this transition while leaving that question open, provided we commit to a clear rule and timely notice for everyone.

Access also limits what the bed count alone can tell us. Two of the twenty full beds are raised beds reserved for gardeners who need them, and neither is among the four becoming vacant. My proposal preserves that reservation and leaves the existing access assessment unchanged. A standard half bed is not automatically a substitute for a raised bed merely because its area can be counted in the same way.

The location of the vacancies presents a further objection: all four are at the far end of the site, so all eight new households would begin in the same area. Voluntary exchanges with returning members might help, but they are not guaranteed and should not be counted as part of what this proposal delivers. Nor should a new household have to negotiate a private favor to obtain a usable route to its bed. Before making offers, the committee should check the paths to the new half beds and report any access problem it cannot resolve. The concentration of new members in one area remains a drawback even if those routes are usable.

Offers would follow the waiting list’s current order. Preserving that order also preserves whatever disadvantages households faced in learning about the list; it is not a claim that everyone had an equal opportunity to join it. But changing the order during this allocation would introduce another contested decision without advance notice. We should begin reviewing how the list is advertised now and announce any future change to its ordering before that change applies.

The choice before us is therefore a limited transition with a visible cost. Dividing the vacancies would make eight offers possible while leaving two waiting households without a bed if all offers are accepted. Immediately dividing occupied beds might create more places, but it would spread disruption across more gardeners and established crops. I support starting with vacancies, preserving the raised-bed reservation and current waiting-list order, checking access before offers, and publishing the next season’s rule before renewals open. The meeting should weigh the remaining queue and the disruption to existing planting together; neither cost disappears because we choose the other.

**Theorem.** Let \((a_n)_{n\ge1}\) be a nonnegative, nonincreasing real sequence with limit zero, and define
\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then \(d_n\ge0\) for every \(n\), and
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1.
\]
For every integer \(N\ge1\), the tail after \(N\) terms is
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, this tail is less than any prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\) when \(N\) is sufficiently large.

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\ge a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\ge0\).

To understand the infinite series, first consider its partial sum of \(N\) terms. The intermediate terms cancel:
\[
S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})
=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\]
Thus
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}.
\]
Because \(a_n\to0\), this difference tends to zero. In other words, the partial sums approach \(a_1\). This is precisely what it means for the series to converge to \(a_1\).

Now fix \(N\ge1\). For every integer \(M>N\), the same cancellation gives
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})
=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\]
The difference between this finite tail sum and \(a_{N+1}\) is \(a_{M+1}\), which tends to zero as \(M\to\infty\). Hence the infinite tail exists and equals
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]

Finally, given \(\varepsilon>0\), the assumption \(a_n\to0\) provides an integer \(K\ge1\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) whenever \(k\ge K\). For every \(N\ge K\), therefore,
\[
0\le\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
All cancellations remain valid when some or all terms are equal; no strict decrease is needed. \(\square\)

\[

\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is an \(N\geq 1\) for which this tail is less than \(\varepsilon\).

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\geq a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\geq 0\).

To find the sum of the series, consider its first \(N\) terms. Substituting the definition of \(d_n\), all intermediate terms cancel:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_N:=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
&=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})\\
&=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the distance from the partial sum to \(a_1\) is
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}.
\]
Because \(a_n\) tends to zero, this distance tends to zero. More explicitly, given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose an integer \(K\geq 1\) such that
\[
a_k<\varepsilon\qquad\text{whenever }k\geq K.
\]
Then, for every \(N\geq K\),
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
The partial sums therefore converge to \(a_1\), which is precisely what it means for the series to converge to \(a_1\).

Now fix an integer \(N\geq 1\). For any integer \(M>N\), the same cancellation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{N,M}:=\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
&=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})\\
&=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
|T_{N,M}-a_{N+1}|=a_{M+1}.
\]
Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(K\) as above. Whenever \(M\geq\max\{N+1,K\}\), this distance is less than \(\varepsilon\). Hence the finite tail sums converge to \(a_{N+1}\), so
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
Finally, taking any \(N\geq K\) gives
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]

The cancellation identities also hold when consecutive terms are equal, in which case the corresponding \(d_n\) is zero. If \(a_1=0\), nonnegativity and monotonicity force every \(a_n\) to be zero, and the same proof applies. \(\square\)

The compost thermometer has returned from its brief career as a dibber. It is back on the hook inside the shed, where it can resume measuring temperature rather than making holes. Please use the wooden dibbers for planting. They have fewer opinions about heat.

This month we are comparing the middle of the active heap with its outer edge. On your rota day, take one reading at each marked position and record both on the sheet. Push the probe to the mark on its shaft, wait until the display settles, and wipe it before returning it to the hook. If the display never settles, write that down instead of choosing the number you like best.

A warmer middle is interesting, but a single pair of readings will not tell us whether the whole heap is ready to use. We are collecting observations over the month. The stewards will also inspect the material before deciding whether to open the bay for collection. Until the notice changes, please keep adding suitable material to the active bay and leave the resting bay alone.

The recording sheet has room for comments because weather, recently added material, and an uncooperative display may help explain a reading. You do not need to write a small novel. “Heavy rain this morning” is useful. “The heap has entered a troubled period” is less useful, though we appreciate the concern.
